title: Python analysis
text:
I used the nycflights23 dataset to explore how average departure delays differed between airlines operating flights from New York City airports in 2023.
Data source: The flight data come from the nycflights13 pyython package (Chow, Michael), licensed under CC0. The dataset contains flight information for flights departing from New York City airports.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from nycflights13 import flights



First, I grouped the flights by airline and calculated the average departure delay for each carrier. I also counted the number of flights operated by each airline. Missing departure-delay values were excluded from the calculation of the average.

carrier_delays = (
    flights
    .groupby("carrier")
    .agg(
        avg_dep_delay=("dep_delay", "mean"),
        n_flights=("carrier", "size")
    )
    .reset_index()
    .sort_values("avg_dep_delay", ascending=False)
)

Overall, this analysis demonstrates how grouping, summarising, and visualization can be used to investigate patterns in flight delays using Python.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Still catching my breath from undergrad graduation, standing at the same sign that’s now the start of a new chapter.


The first weeks of the program have been a different kind of intensity. Between programming for data science and statistics and probability, I’ve gone from “comfortable with code” to relearning how to think about problems the way this program wants me to: rigorously and reproducibly.
Even with that intensity, I’ve been lucky to meet really interesting people who are in the same boat. We’re sharing this experience together, and I’m grateful for that. Coming from such a diverse range of backgrounds, it feels good to be able to rely on them — and to be relied on — even though we only met a few weeks ago.

title: R analysis
text:
I used the nycflights23 dataset to explore how average departure delays differed between airlines operating flights from New York City airports in 2023.
Data source: The flight data come from the nycflights23 R package (Ismay, Couch, & Wickham, 2025), licensed under CC0, which provides flight information for flights departing from New York City airports in 2023.

library(tidyverse)
library(nycflights23)



First, I grouped the flights by airline and calculated the average departure delay for each carrier. I also counted the number of flights operated by each airline. Missing departure-delay values were excluded from the calculation of the average.

carrier_delays <- flights |>
  group_by(carrier) |>
  summarise(
    avg_dep_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_flights = n()
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_dep_delay))

carrier_delays

Overall, this analysis demonstrates how grouping, summarising, and visualization can be used to investigate patterns in flight delays using R.

title: About
text: I’m originally from Mexico and have called Canada home for the past 8 years. I completed my undergraduate degree at UBC with a Combined Major in Microbiology and Computer Science, a mix that I wasn’t sure I would like at first, but eventually became a passion. Before starting MDS, I worked at a geochemical laboratory, where I spent my days doing high-throughput analytical work. That job is actually what pushed me toward this program: I kept finding the data side of the work more interesting than anything else, and wanted to build the skills to do more of it.

title: About
text:
Why Data Science
After years of generating data in the lab, I wanted to be just as comfortable analyzing it. MDS felt like the natural next step, a chance to formalize the programming skills I’d picked up and turn into an actual data scientist. I’m especially interested in where data science meets biology, and I’m using this program to build toward data-driven roles that let me keep working at that intersection.

title: About
text:
Outside of Data Science
Outside of code and coursework, I love dancing (mostly latin dance). I also enjoy a good walk and reading about history. I’d describe myself as a curious mind at heart: I like understanding how things work, whether that’s a dataset, a genome, or a new hobby, one piece at a time.
